summary: Explains why it can be useful to extend IPsec with a mode that does not authenticate peers: deploying authentication credentials is often a big obstacle to using IPsec at all. It sets out the problem and applicability for Better-Than-Nothing Security. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: Setting up name tags for everybody is hard work, so many people skip locking their doors altogether. This memo argues that a lock without name tags is still better than no lock.

questions: what is better than nothing security
subtitle: Why IPsec without peer authentication can still be better than no security, and when to use it.

tldr.problem: IPsec and IKE require authentication, and deploying identities and credentials is often such a hurdle that people skip network-layer security entirely.
tldr.mechanism: Better-Than-Nothing Security (BTNS) lets IPsec set up security associations without network-layer authentication. Stand-Alone BTNS (SAB) relies on IPsec alone, while Channel-Bound BTNS (CBB) ties the association to authentication done at a higher layer.
tldr.outcome: BTNS protects a session once it is established but not its setup, so it should replace no security, never stronger security. It suits open services and long-lived connections.

facts.label: Default meaning of SAB or CBB

today: RFC 5387 is an Informational RFC (November 2008), and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The detailed IPsec extension is specified separately in RFC 5386.

sections.title: The Problem: Authentication Is a Hurdle
sections.content:
IPsec (IKE, ESP and AH) secures IP traffic, but authentication is required. Authentication needs identities and credentials, such as pre-shared secrets or certificates signed by a certification authority, which often take manual coordination and significant time and effort. As a result, some users rely on higher-layer protocols such as TLS, or use no security.

Higher layers are not always enough. Transport protocols like TCP are open to off-path attacks such as an injected RST, and the Internet lacks comprehensive ingress filtering. The RFC notes that this was a concern for BGP sessions, and it says BGP was a motivation for BTNS even though the routing community chose other solutions such as TCP MD5. Protocols such as iSCSI authenticate above IPsec, which means two separate authentications that must be kept consistent, or an attacker can act as a proxy.

BTNS removes the network-layer authentication requirement. It uses a weaker notion called continuity of association: the entity you are talking to now is the same one as before on this security association (SA). It holds only for the life of one SA.
sections.plainLanguage: Checking everyone's ID is so much work that people skip locks entirely. BTNS keeps the lock but drops the ID check, so at least nobody new can barge into a conversation that has already started.

sections.title: SAB, CBB and Channel Binding
sections.content:
Stand-Alone BTNS (SAB) protects traffic from a higher-layer protocol that does not authenticate. Once an unauthenticated SA is created without a man-in-the-middle (MITM), its services resist later MITM attacks, even though the creation itself can be subverted.

Channel-Bound BTNS (CBB) protects traffic from a protocol that does authenticate. Connection latching and channel binding tie the IPsec SAs to the higher-layer session, creating an IPsec channel. If an attacker concatenates two SAs as a proxy, the higher-layer authentication fails and the session is terminated. Protection can then be comparable to network-layer IKE authentication when the higher layer is strong.

Either mode can be symmetric (neither side authenticates at the network layer) or asymmetric (only one side does not). Unqualified, the symmetric mode is meant. Channel binding must be applied at both ends.
sections.plainLanguage: SAB is a lock with no ID check at all. CBB is a lock where you check IDs later, through a different door, and make sure it is the same person who came in through the lock.

sections.title: What BTNS Changes in IPsec
sections.content:
The main change is to security policy. In the Peer Authorization Database (PAD), an unauthenticated category is added where the peer's public key serves as its identity. A flag is added to each Security Policy Database (SPD) entry to say whether BTNS is acceptable. Other parts of IPsec and IKE are unchanged, and non-BTNS entries and SAs are unaffected. Channel binding between IPsec and higher layers needs APIs, which this document assumes will be developed but does not specify.

For security services, access control is extended to allow unauthenticated connections, and data origin authentication weakens to continuity of association under SAB. Integrity, anti-replay and confidentiality still apply once a connection exists, in the same way as for conventional IPsec, though a rogue peer can set one up.
sections.plainLanguage: BTNS only adds a switch on each rule that says it is fine to skip the ID check here. Everything else works the way it did.

sections.title: When to Use Each Mode
sections.content:
BTNS suits services open to the public that still want protected associations, services that can be authenticated at higher layers, and private services where the alternative is no protection. It should not be used where IPsec or IKE is unsuitable, for example with limited computation or high latency.

SAB fits applications that cannot use IKE credentials and have no other authentication, particularly long-lived connections such as large file transfers that should not be cut by a false TCP RST. Symmetric examples include open web servers, peer-to-peer networks, VoIP and BGP sessions between core routers. Asymmetric SAB suits a web server authenticated by a well-known CA with anonymous clients. CBB suits applications with their own authentication, such as iSCSI and NFS.

Benefits: no pre-deployed authentication material, protection for all transport protocols, and attackers forced to do as much work as a legitimate host. Vulnerabilities: masqueraders (until higher layers bind, for CBB), resource load, and exposure to open access. Traffic selectors and rate limiting can restrict access.
sections.plainLanguage: Use it for places anyone may visit, like a shop, or for long phone calls you do not want cut off. Do not use it where you really need to know who is on the other end.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
BTNS protects a session once established but not the key exchange, so a MITM can take part in setup. SAB does not protect against masquerading clients. CBB detects a MITM only later, when the higher-layer authentication fails, so it must not be used with higher-layer protocols that expose sensitive material, such as passwords or data open to off-line attack. BTNS also does not protect against DoS attacks on computation or against configuration mistakes.

BTNS should be a substitute for no security, preferably instead of "bypass" SPD entries, never for stronger security. SAB implies the service is open to anyone. Rekeying can let an on-path attacker hijack the new SA, which SAB makes easier and CBB can detect. The RFC compares BTNS to SSH's "Leap of Faith": SSH warns and allows rejection, while BTNS accepts credentials automatically when policy permits.
sections.plainLanguage: The lock only works once the door is shut. A trickster who gets in at the very start can still fool you, so only use it where the alternative is no lock at all.
